Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 105, verse 1–5:

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: It was revealed in Makkah: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾.

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

The interrogative in His words, ﴿Have you not considered﴾, serves to affirm his ﷺ seeing (of it) by denying its absence.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning is, "Have you not been informed?"

Al-Zajjāj said: "Have you not known?" It is an expression of wonder directed at him ﷺ regarding what Allah did to ﴿the companions of the elephant﴾, those who intended to destroy the Kaʿbah from among the Abyssinians. "How" (kayfa) is in the accusative by the verb following it, and it suspends the verb of seeing. The address is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it may also be to everyone who is fit for it.

The meaning: "You have known, O Muhammad, or the people existing in your era and those after them have known, through the widely transmitted reports that reached you, the story of the companions of the elephant and what Allah did to them. So why do you not believe?" The elephant (al-fīl) is the well-known animal; its plural is afyāl, fuyūl and fīlah.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: one does not say afīlah, and its handler is fayyāl. The story of the companions of the elephant will be mentioned later, if Allah wills.

﴿Did He not make their plot into misguidance?﴾ That is: did He not make their scheming and their effort to destroy the Kaʿbah and to violate its people into misguidance, from what they aimed at, so that they did not reach the House nor what they intended by their plot? The hamzah is for affirmation, as if it were said: "He has indeed made their plot into misguidance." The plot (kayd) is the intention to harm another, for they intended to plot against Quraysh by killing and capturing, and to plot against the Sacred House by destroying it.

﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ That is, groups following one another, like camels gathered in herds.

Abū ʿUbayda said: "abābīl" means groups in dispersal; it is said, "The horses came abābīl," meaning groups from here and from there.

Al-Naḥḥās said: its real meaning is that they were great groups. It is said, "Fulān wabala ʿalā Fulān," meaning he exalted himself over him and became proud. It is derived from the camels, and it is a plural with no singular.

Some said: its singular is abūl, like ʿajūl.

Some said: abīl.

Al-Wāḥidī said: "We have not seen anyone assign a singular to it."

Al-Farrāʾ said: it has no singular from its own form.

Al-Ruʾāsī, who was trustworthy, claimed that he heard its singular as ibbālah with a shaddah.

Al-Farrāʾ also related: abālah with a light (unstressed) form.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: they were birds from the sky the like of which had not been seen before or after.

Qatādah said: they were black birds that came from the direction of the sea in flocks, flock after flock, each bird with three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak, which strikes nothing without crushing it.

It was also said they were green birds that emerged from the sea, having heads like the heads of beasts of prey.

It was also said they had the beaks of birds and paws like dogs' paws.

Other descriptions were given, and the Arabs use abābīl for birds, as in the words of the poet:

"You see them rushing to the caller, as if they were abābīl of birds beneath a sheltering cloud,"

and they use it for other than birds, as in the words of another:

"My mount nearly broke from the cries when I asked the earth with the swift abābīl."

﴿Pelting them with stones of sijjīl﴾ The clause is in the position of an accusative as a description of "birds."

The majority read tarmīhim with the feminine (second person) form. Abū Ḥanīfah, Abū Maʿmar, ʿĪsā and Ṭalḥah read it with the masculine (third person) form, and a collective noun may be masculine or feminine.

It was said: the pronoun in the second reading refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Zajjāj said: ﴿of sijjīl﴾ means: of what He had written as punishment for them, derived from the sijill (register).

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: they said it is a stone of clay baked in the fire of Hell, on which the names of the people are written.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abzā said: ﴿of sijjīl﴾ means from the sky, and it is the stones that fell upon the people of Lūṭ. It was also said: from the Jaḥīm, which is Sijjīn; then the nūn was changed into lām. From this is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

"A blow with which the champions have agreed upon sijjīlan"

while the original is "sijjīnā."

ʿIkrimah said: they pelted them with stones carried with them; when one of the stones struck one of them, the smallpox came out with it. The stone was like a chickpea and larger than a lentil. We have already discussed sijjīl in Surah Hūd.

﴿So He made them like eaten stalks﴾ That is, Allah made the companions of the elephant like the leaves of crops when the animals have eaten them and thrown them out from below; he likened the cutting apart of their limbs to the scattering of its parts.

It was also said the meaning is: they became like leaves of a crop from which animals have eaten and some remnants remained, or they ate its grain and it remained without its grain.

ʿAṣf is the plural of ʿaṣfah, ʿuṣāfah and ʿaṣīfah. We have already discussed ʿaṣf in Surah al-Raḥmān, so refer back to it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqī have narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The companions of the elephant came until they alighted at al-Ṣifāḥ, and ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib came to them and said: "This is the House of Allah; He has not given anyone power over it." They said: "We will not return until we demolish it." They would not advance their elephant except that it would hold back. So he (Allah) called upon the birds, the abābīl, and gave them black stones with clay upon them. When they came level with them, they pelted them, and none of them remained except that he was seized by itching, so that a man would not scratch his skin without his flesh falling off.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim, Abū Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqī have narrated from him: The companions of the elephant advanced until, when they drew near to Makkah, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib met them. He said to their king: "What brought you to us? Why did you not send for us, so that we might come to you with everything?" He said: "I have been told about this House, which no one enters without being safe, so I came to frighten its people." He said: "We will bring you everything you want; return." But he refused except to enter it, and he set off moving toward it. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib stayed behind, stood upon a mountain and said: "I do not witness the destruction of this House and its people." Then there came like a cloud from the direction of the sea until it overshadowed them, the birds, the abābīl, of which Allah said: ﴿pelting them with stones of sijjīl﴾, and the elephant began to bellow, ﴿so He made them like eaten stalks﴾. The story of the companions of the elephant is extensively and at length set out in the books of history and biographies, so we will not lengthen it by mentioning it.

Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿pelting them with stones of sijjīl﴾, he said: "stones like hazelnuts, with a red mark stamped upon them; with each bird three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak. It hovered over them from the sky, then sent those stones upon them, and they did not pass beyond their army."

Abū Nuʿaym also narrated through the route of ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk from him that Abraha al-Ashram came from Yemen wanting to demolish the Kaʿbah, so Allah sent against them birds, abābīl, meaning gathered together, which had beaks carrying a pebble in their beaks and two pebbles in their feet; they would release one upon the head of a man, and his flesh and blood would flow, and bones would remain hollow, with no flesh upon them, no skin and no blood.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil also narrated from him: ﴿So He made them like eaten stalks﴾, he says: like chaff.

Ibn Isḥāq in the Sīrah, al-Wāqidī, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqī narrated from ʿĀʾishah, who said: "I saw the leader of the elephant and its driver in Makkah, both blind and crippled, begging for food."

al-Wāqidī narrated something similar from Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr.

Abū Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was born in the Year of the Elephant."

Ibn Isḥāq, Abū Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqī narrated "from Qays ibn Makhramah, who said: I and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were born in the Year of the Elephant."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 105, verse 1–5:

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: It was revealed in Makkah: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾.

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

The interrogative in His words, ﴿Have you not considered﴾, serves to affirm his ﷺ seeing (of it) by denying its absence.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the meaning is, "Have you not been informed?"

Al-Zajjāj said: "Have you not known?" It is an expression of wonder directed at him ﷺ regarding what Allah did to ﴿the companions of the elephant﴾, those who intended to destroy the Kaʿbah from among the Abyssinians. "How" (kayfa) is in the accusative by the verb following it, and it suspends the verb of seeing. The address is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it may also be to everyone who is fit for it.

The meaning: "You have known, O Muhammad, or the people existing in your era and those after them have known, through the widely transmitted reports that reached you, the story of the companions of the elephant and what Allah did to them. So why do you not believe?" The elephant (al-fīl) is the well-known animal; its plural is afyāl, fuyūl and fīlah.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: one does not say afīlah, and its handler is fayyāl. The story of the companions of the elephant will be mentioned later, if Allah wills.

﴿Did He not make their plot into misguidance?﴾ That is: did He not make their scheming and their effort to destroy the Kaʿbah and to violate its people into misguidance, from what they aimed at, so that they did not reach the House nor what they intended by their plot? The hamzah is for affirmation, as if it were said: "He has indeed made their plot into misguidance." The plot (kayd) is the intention to harm another, for they intended to plot against Quraysh by killing and capturing, and to plot against the Sacred House by destroying it.

﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ That is, groups following one another, like camels gathered in herds.

Abū ʿUbayda said: "abābīl" means groups in dispersal; it is said, "The horses came abābīl," meaning groups from here and from there.

Al-Naḥḥās said: its real meaning is that they were great groups. It is said, "Fulān wabala ʿalā Fulān," meaning he exalted himself over him and became proud. It is derived from the camels, and it is a plural with no singular.

Some said: its singular is abūl, like ʿajūl.

Some said: abīl.

Al-Wāḥidī said: "We have not seen anyone assign a singular to it."

Al-Farrāʾ said: it has no singular from its own form.

Al-Ruʾāsī, who was trustworthy, claimed that he heard its singular as ibbālah with a shaddah.

Al-Farrāʾ also related: abālah with a light (unstressed) form.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: they were birds from the sky the like of which had not been seen before or after.

Qatādah said: they were black birds that came from the direction of the sea in flocks, flock after flock, each bird with three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak, which strikes nothing without crushing it.

It was also said they were green birds that emerged from the sea, having heads like the heads of beasts of prey.

It was also said they had the beaks of birds and paws like dogs' paws.

Other descriptions were given, and the Arabs use abābīl for birds, as in the words of the poet:

"You see them rushing to the caller, as if they were abābīl of birds beneath a sheltering cloud,"

and they use it for other than birds, as in the words of another:

"My mount nearly broke from the cries when I asked the earth with the swift abābīl."

﴿Pelting them with stones of sijjīl﴾ The clause is in the position of an accusative as a description of "birds."

The majority read tarmīhim with the feminine (second person) form. Abū Ḥanīfah, Abū Maʿmar, ʿĪsā and Ṭalḥah read it with the masculine (third person) form, and a collective noun may be masculine or feminine.

It was said: the pronoun in the second reading refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Zajjāj said: ﴿of sijjīl﴾ means: of what He had written as punishment for them, derived from the sijill (register).

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: they said it is a stone of clay baked in the fire of Hell, on which the names of the people are written.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abzā said: ﴿of sijjīl﴾ means from the sky, and it is the stones that fell upon the people of Lūṭ. It was also said: from the Jaḥīm, which is Sijjīn; then the nūn was changed into lām. From this is the saying of Ibn Muqbil:

"A blow with which the champions have agreed upon sijjīlan"

while the original is "sijjīnā."

ʿIkrimah said: they pelted them with stones carried with them; when one of the stones struck one of them, the smallpox came out with it. The stone was like a chickpea and larger than a lentil. We have already discussed sijjīl in Surah Hūd.

﴿So He made them like eaten stalks﴾ That is, Allah made the companions of the elephant like the leaves of crops when the animals have eaten them and thrown them out from below; he likened the cutting apart of their limbs to the scattering of its parts.

It was also said the meaning is: they became like leaves of a crop from which animals have eaten and some remnants remained, or they ate its grain and it remained without its grain.

ʿAṣf is the plural of ʿaṣfah, ʿuṣāfah and ʿaṣīfah. We have already discussed ʿaṣf in Surah al-Raḥmān, so refer back to it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqī have narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The companions of the elephant came until they alighted at al-Ṣifāḥ, and ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib came to them and said: "This is the House of Allah; He has not given anyone power over it." They said: "We will not return until we demolish it." They would not advance their elephant except that it would hold back. So he (Allah) called upon the birds, the abābīl, and gave them black stones with clay upon them. When they came level with them, they pelted them, and none of them remained except that he was seized by itching, so that a man would not scratch his skin without his flesh falling off.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim, Abū Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqī have narrated from him: The companions of the elephant advanced until, when they drew near to Makkah, ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib met them. He said to their king: "What brought you to us? Why did you not send for us, so that we might come to you with everything?" He said: "I have been told about this House, which no one enters without being safe, so I came to frighten its people." He said: "We will bring you everything you want; return." But he refused except to enter it, and he set off moving toward it. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib stayed behind, stood upon a mountain and said: "I do not witness the destruction of this House and its people." Then there came like a cloud from the direction of the sea until it overshadowed them, the birds, the abābīl, of which Allah said: ﴿pelting them with stones of sijjīl﴾, and the elephant began to bellow, ﴿so He made them like eaten stalks﴾. The story of the companions of the elephant is extensively and at length set out in the books of history and biographies, so we will not lengthen it by mentioning it.

Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words, ﴿pelting them with stones of sijjīl﴾, he said: "stones like hazelnuts, with a red mark stamped upon them; with each bird three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak. It hovered over them from the sky, then sent those stones upon them, and they did not pass beyond their army."

Abū Nuʿaym also narrated through the route of ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk from him that Abraha al-Ashram came from Yemen wanting to demolish the Kaʿbah, so Allah sent against them birds, abābīl, meaning gathered together, which had beaks carrying a pebble in their beaks and two pebbles in their feet; they would release one upon the head of a man, and his flesh and blood would flow, and bones would remain hollow, with no flesh upon them, no skin and no blood.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil also narrated from him: ﴿So He made them like eaten stalks﴾, he says: like chaff.

Ibn Isḥāq in the Sīrah, al-Wāqidī, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqī narrated from ʿĀʾishah, who said: "I saw the leader of the elephant and its driver in Makkah, both blind and crippled, begging for food."

al-Wāqidī narrated something similar from Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr.

Abū Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was born in the Year of the Elephant."

Ibn Isḥāq, Abū Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqī narrated "from Qays ibn Makhramah, who said: I and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were born in the Year of the Elephant."
